vignette: Mr. Thompson is a 71-year-old married security guard who has been grappling with the aftermath of a terrorist attack at his workplace several months ago. The traumatic event left an indelible mark on him, manifesting in persistent and distressing symptoms. The incident occurred during his night shift when he was alone in the building. An individual armed with a knife entered through a side door that Mr. Thompson had mistakenly left unlocked earlier. Despite his efforts to remain composed and alert, the assailant cornered him in one of the rooms. The attack lasted only minutes but felt like an eternity as he fought for his life. Since then, Mr. Thompson has found himself unable to shake off the memories of this terrifying ordeal. His recollections are vivid and detailed; every sound, every movement of the attacker seems etched into his mind. However, at times, these memories feel emotionally detached, almost as if they happened to someone else. He struggles to piece together a coherent narrative of what transpired that night, which only adds to his confusion and distress. Mr. Thompson's sense of self has been profoundly shaken by this event. He harbors deep-seated negative appraisals about himself and his ability to cope with life’s challenges. He believes he cannot handle even the slightest upset without crumbling under pressure. This pervasive feeling of inadequacy is compounded by his belief that someone else would have handled the situation differently, perhaps more competently. He feels like he has failed in his most important role as a security guard and as a husband. These negative appraisals fuel Mr. Thompson’s maladaptive strategies for managing his anxiety. He now insists on sitting with his back against walls wherever he goes to maintain a full view of the room, ensuring no one can approach him from behind without being seen. This behavior has extended beyond work into his home life, where he often positions himself in such a way that he feels more secure. His rumination about how to get even with the assailant also stems from these negative appraisals. He spends considerable time imagining scenarios of retribution, which only serves to heighten his hypervigilance towards potentially dangerous individuals. This constant state of alertness has taken a toll on him, making it difficult for him to relax or engage in activities that once brought him joy. These maladaptive strategies have also affected how he processes and recalls the traumatic event. The vividness of his memories is exacerbated by his hypervigilance, leading to intrusive thoughts and flashbacks that disrupt his daily life. His rumination about revenge further compounds this, as it keeps the memory fresh in his mind, making it difficult for him to move past what happened. In addition to these symptoms, Mr. Thompson has become increasingly isolated from others, even within his marriage. He avoids discussing the event with anyone, including his wife, who feels distant and frustrated by his reluctance to open up. This isolation has strained their relationship, leaving both parties feeling unsupported. The cumulative effect of these maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals is a cycle that continues to tighten around Mr. Thompson. His inability to cope effectively and the belief that he has failed in his role exacerbate his anxiety and hypervigilance, which in turn make it more difficult for him to process his memories and integrate them into his life narrative. What finally brought Mr. Thompson to seek help was a realization that his current coping mechanisms were not sustainable. He was certain that if he continued down this path, his relationships and overall quality of life would suffer further. Despite his fears about opening up and reliving the trauma, he hopes for a way to regain control over his life and find some semblance of peace.
